description: Interested in astronomy, solving problems and having fun!
summary: Stratofall is a browser game about jumping from a balloon capsule in the stratosphere. You step off at 21 to 39 km, control your spin in thin air, answer suit warnings, open your canopy in the right height window and land inside a ring on the ground. The air in the game gets thicker as you fall. That changes your top speed, your Mach number and how much you can steer. The game shows how a stratospheric jump works, step by step, and what can go wrong.
details:
What it does

Each jump has four phases:

  1. Exit. The capsule sways. You press jump while the sway marker is in the green. A bad exit starts you spinning.
  2. Freefall. You keep the spin near zero, steer toward the landing zone and answer timed warnings. You can dive head-down to go faster, but it makes you less stable.
  3. Canopy. The canopy is locked above 2,500 m. The best window is 1,500 to 900 m. If you open too fast (over 78 m/s, about 280 km/h), while spinning (over 25 rpm) or in a dive, the canopy tears. Depending on the level you may need to kick out line twists or cut away a failed main canopy and open the reserve.
  4. Landing. You steer into the ring, face into the wind and flare at about 6 m.

The warnings are suit and mission problems: visor fogging, suit pressure drop, low oxygen flow, a call from mission control, a glove heater fault and a stuck vent valve. Each one asks for a key (or a short key sequence on later levels) before a timer runs out. A missed warning takes 14 to 34% off the suit. If the suit reaches 0%, the jump ends. A missed visor warning also fogs the view for a few seconds.

Every failure screen says what went wrong and what to do next time. There are nine endings: blackout from spin, suit failure, no canopy, opened too low, canopy failure, line twist, hard landing, tumbling on landing and missing the ring.

Each jump gives up to three stars: land safely in the ring; reach a speed goal (800 km/h on jump 1, then Mach 1.0, 1.05, 1.17 and 1.32); and land close to the centre, softly (under 3 m/s) and with no missed warnings.

It works with a keyboard or with touch controls (written for iPad). It has a chase camera and a helmet view. Progress is saved in the browser.

How it works

The game is one HTML file. It uses Three.js for the 3D scene and plain JavaScript for the simulation. There is no server and no build step.

Air density. Density falls with height using a single exponential: 1.225 kg/m³ at the ground, with a scale height of 7,200 m. This is a simple textbook-style approximation. It is not a full standard-atmosphere table.

Drag and terminal velocity. Drag grows with the square of speed and with air density. At ground level, terminal velocity is 55 m/s in a belly-down arch and 104 m/s in a head-down dive. Because drag scales with density, the same body falls much faster in thin air. So you speed up quickly near the top, reach your peak speed high up, and slow down as the air thickens.

Speed of sound and Mach. The speed of sound drops in a straight line from 340 m/s at the ground to 295 m/s at 11 km. Above 11 km it stays at 295 m/s. Mach number is your speed divided by that value. A visual ring and a sound play when you first pass Mach 1.

Control authority. How well you can steer depends on how much drag you have compared with your weight. High up, where the air is thin, steering is almost zero. The in-game coach says so: "Thin air: no steering yet."

Spin. Random twisting forces push on the jumper. They are stronger in thin air (from about 7 km to 20 km and above), stronger in a dive and stronger in turbulence. There are also random kicks above 6 km. Thicker air damps the spin when you are arched. The player counters with spin-left and spin-right keys. Above 55 rpm a blackout meter fills. If it fills completely, you black out.

Wind. Each level has a base wind with gusts. The wind turns with height (shear). Some levels add a jet stream: a band of strong wind centred at 10.5 km, about 2.6 km thick. The wind pushes you sideways in freefall and under canopy. A wind arrow on the screen shows the direction.

Canopy. Inflation takes 2.2 seconds (1.6 seconds for the reserve). During that time your sink rate eases from your falling speed down to 6.3 m/s. When open, the canopy flies forward at about 12 m/s. Braking slows you down; diving speeds you up; turning adds sink. The reserve is a little slower and sinks a little faster. A failed main sinks at 38 m/s. After a cutaway you are back in freefall until you open the reserve.

Flare and landing. You can flare below 40 m. A flare brings the sink rate down to 1.2 m/s for about 2.6 seconds, then the canopy stalls. Flare too early and you land hard. A landing fails if the vertical speed is over 5.2 m/s, the ground speed is over 9.5 m/s, or you land outside the ring.

Graphics. The sky changes from blue to black between about 9 km and 30 km, and stars fade in. The ground uses three photo textures at different scales, plus haze that depends on height. A cloud layer sits at a different height on each level. The ground curves away to show the horizon. The suit, capsule, balloon and canopy are built from simple 3D shapes in code. A code comment credits these models to "Astra" [confirm who or what this is]. The mission badge on the suit is fictional and drawn in code.

Sound. All sound effects are generated live in the browser with the Web Audio API. There are no audio files.

What is simplified or exaggerated

We want to be clear about what is real and what is a game choice.

  • Time runs faster. Freefall runs at 3 times real time, so a jump fits in a few minutes. Under canopy, time runs up to 4 times faster high up and slows to 1.4 times near the ground, so the landing stays playable.
  • Earth's curve is exaggerated. The game uses an Earth radius of 3,000 km, about half the real value, so the curve of the horizon is easy to see from 20 to 39 km. The code comment says this is on purpose.
  • The atmosphere is a simple formula. Density is one exponential curve and the speed of sound is a straight line plus a constant. Real temperature, pressure and wind profiles are not used.
  • Wind is made up. Wind speed, direction, gusts and the jet stream are numbers chosen for each level. They do not come from weather data.
  • Spin, warnings and failures are game mechanics. The spin forces are random. The warnings come at random heights. The suit damage values, the keys and the canopy failure on jump 4 are chosen for play, not taken from a real suit or mission.
  • Supersonic goals on later levels. The Mach goals rise with each level. [Confirm whether these targets are reachable in normal play; the source code alone does not show this.]
  • Cold, pressure and oxygen are not simulated. They only appear as warning cards.

Benefits

  • It shows, by playing, why a jump from the stratosphere is different from a normal skydive: thin air means high speed and very little control.
  • It links each danger to a clear cause and a fix. The failure screens explain what happened in plain words.
  • It runs in a browser on a laptop or iPad, with nothing to install.
  • It walks through the full sequence of a high-altitude jump: checklist, exit, freefall, canopy, malfunction handling and landing.

Intended impact

We want players, especially students, to get a feel for how the atmosphere changes with height and why it matters for anyone coming back down from near space. The game is a starting point for talking about air density, terminal velocity, the speed of sound and wind at altitude.

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework, no build step)
  • Three.js r128, loaded from cdnjs
  • WebGL with custom GLSL shaders for the sky, ground, clouds and landing ring
  • Web Audio API for all sound
  • Browser localStorage for saved progress
  • Google Fonts: Saira, Saira Condensed and Share Tech Mono
  • Published as a Claude artifact (claude.ai)
  • [Tools used to make the four texture images]
  • [Tool used to record and edit the demo video]

Creativity

  • The jump is built around one key (space) that does three jobs: jump, open the canopy and flare. Its meaning changes with the phase.
  • The physics is the level design. Thin air makes steering useless high up, so the player has to manage spin first and steer later.
  • Timed warning cards stand in for the suit and radio problems a real jumper would have to handle.
  • The game has a helmet view as well as a chase camera.
  • The levels form a ladder from a gentle 21 km jump to a 39 km jump with every problem at once.

Factors we considered

  • Clarity over realism where they conflict. We sped up time and exaggerated Earth's curve on purpose, and we say so above.
  • Teaching through failure. Every ending explains its cause and the fix.
  • Access. Keyboard and touch controls, two camera views, a sound on/off switch. If the device's "reduce motion" setting is on, the camera does not spin with the jumper and does not shake.
  • Performance. Lower pixel ratio on touch devices, simple shapes for models and no shadows.
  • No server and no personal data. The only thing stored is level progress, in the player's own browser.
